title: What Is the Most Human Aspect of Leadership
author: Tim Draayer
source: The Inner Call (Tim Draayer Substack), January 12, 2026
summary: Draayer asks what is most human about leadership and rejects the assumption that all leadership behaviours are equally human just because leadership is a human concept. Manipulation, cajoling, and other means of reaching a goal are human behaviours but they subtract from others' lived experience rather than adding to it; that subtraction is what disqualifies them from the most-human category. The criterion he names is simple: good leaders add to the work environment and home, takers subtract. From there he gives a short list of aspects he treats as the most human dimensions: connection, trust, empathy, authenticity, inclusivity, humour, culture, and safety. The piece's posture is reflective rather than prescriptive: start with the aspects you feel drawn to, grade yourself honestly (am I being authentic at work or pretending to be someone I am not?), then convert the introspection into improvement (sometimes as simple as remembering to smile more; sometimes more substantial reading on aligning actions with values). Draayer closes with a faith framing — look to God to lead you to the resources to become the leader you were created to be — situating leadership formation as a practice of self-examination plus action.
points: Not every leadership behaviour is equally human; manipulation and cajoling are human in origin but subtract from others' lived experience, which disqualifies them from the most-human category.
The clean criterion: good leaders add to the work environment and home; takers subtract. The frame applies the same way at home as at work.
Draayer's list of most-human leadership dimensions: connection, trust, empathy, authenticity, inclusivity, humour, culture, and safety.
The diagnostic question for each is concrete (am I being authentic at work or pretending to be someone I am not?) rather than abstract; honest self-grading is the entry point.
Improvement runs from small daily moves (remembering to smile more) to deeper alignment work (reading on values-action alignment); the path is iterative rather than total reinvention.
quotes: Leadership is a human concept and we all iterate on our own personal view of being a leader. So by default does that mean any and all aspects of leadership, in all its forms are human? I would argue no.

You don't need to dig too deeply into recent headlines to see examples of dehumanizing and downright evil leaders. Manipulating, cajoling and other means of reaching a goal are human behaviors but do they add or subtract from everyone's lived experience.
That is the key here. Good leaders add to the work environment and/or home. Takers subtract.
For me, the most human aspects of leadership include connection and trust but there are more aspects to be considered. Empathy, Authenticity, Inclusivity, Humor, Culture, Safety.
Be kind to yourself but grade yourself honestly. For example, am I being authentic at work or am I pretending to be someone I am not?

Take the knowledge you glean from the introspection seek ways to improve and grow. Sometimes it might be as simple as remembering to smile more. While other topics might lead you to read articles about aligning actions with your values.” Archived from The Inner Call (Tim Draayer Substack) on May 1, 2026 by Tim.
